events.text: I'm animating a tiny orange campfire spirit doing a happy four-frame bounce because I like game characters that make quiet places feel alive.
Quinn tells where the idea came from

Hello, friends. I wanted to make a tiny campfire spirit because I love the cheerful little creatures in classic 16-bit adventure games, especially the ones that make a quiet forest or campsite feel welcoming. I took inspiration from their simple expressive faces, bright warm colours, and playful idle animations, then imagined a friendly flame who likes to bounce above his own little campfire.

Let's begin with our little friend's wooden base, using the solid box tool to lay down broad, simple shapes on our 32 by 32 pixel grid. I'm choosing warm dark brown, softer wood brown and charcoal grey because those earthy colours will make our bright flame stand out beautifully. The pen tool adds tiny golden brown highlights and near-black shadows, just enough detail to suggest pieces of wood without making them too complicated.

Now I'll take the line tool and draw two little logs stretching diagonally away from the centre. The warm dark brown gives them their main shape, while charcoal grey underneath makes them feel solid and grounded. With the pen, I'm adding two golden brown dots at their outer ends, as though the firelight is gently touching the wood.

Here comes our happy little flame, friends. I'm using the solid box tool to build three overlapping shapes, with orange-red at the bottom, bright orange in the middle, and pale golden yellow at the tip. On our little grid, these straight-edged shapes read as one soft flame, and I'm keeping him narrow and taller than he is wide so he feels light and lively.

Now let's give our spirit his face with the pen tool, one precious dot at a time. Two near-black eyes and a tiny dark brown mouth sit near the lower part of his flame, where they'll remain easy to recognise as he moves. I'm leaving out a nose, eyebrows, and other details because at this small size, a simple friendly expression is all we need.

For our second frame, let's look at the grid and carefully rebuild the wooden base in exactly the same place. I'm using the solid box tool for dark brown, softer brown and charcoal then the pen for golden brown highlights and near-black shadows. Keeping these shapes still will help the viewers see that it's our little flame who is jumping, not the whole campfire.

With the line tool, I'm drawing our two diagonal logs again, using warm dark brown and charcoal grey beneath them. The pen adds those familiar golden brown tips, and I'm checking their positions against the first frame on our grid. Repeating the logs exactly gives the animation a steady foundation.

Now watch our little spirit stretch upward. With the solid box tool, I'm moving his orange-red body, bright orange middle, and pale golden yellow tip two pixels higher, keeping the same basic proportions. The pen adds little orange flickers, and I want this upward stretch to feel like a happy hop rather than a completely different character.

Let's lift his near-black eyes and dark brown mouth along with his body, using the pen tool so every tiny mark stays under control. I'm also placing two little golden yellow sparks beside him, one dot at a time. Those sparks give the jump a playful burst of energy, and because we're keeping the surrounding space empty, even two tiny dots can feel exciting.

Here we are at the third frame, friends, when our flame begins settling downward again. First I'm rebuilding the same wooden base with the solid box tool, using dark brown, medium wood brown and charcoal grey with golden brown highlights and near-black shadow dots from the pen. The proportions stay unchanged because I want our little campsite to feel peaceful beneath all that movement.

Let's draw the familiar logs with the line tool, reaching left and right from the centre. Warm dark brown makes the upper edges, charcoal creates the darker lower edges, and the pen places golden brown dots at their tips. I'm keeping the lines simple and clean because a tiny animated character needs a background that doesn't compete with him.

Now I'll use the solid box tool to place the flame just one pixel below his highest position. His orange-red outer body, bright orange inner shape, and soft yellow tip stay close to their original sizes, and the pen adds two little orange flickers. This small change in height is important, because gentle movement between frames makes a bounce feel smooth rather than jumpy.

With the pen tool, I'm placing his near-black eyes a little lower and drawing a short dark brown mouth with the line tool. Then I'll add two tiny bright orange dots floating beside him. I like how those sparks seem to follow him downward, suggesting that our little friend is made of warm, living fire.

For our final frame, let's build the wooden base once more with the solid box tool. I'm choosing the same dark brown, softer brown and charcoal grey then placing golden brown, light and near-black shadows with the pen. I'll use our grid to keep everything perfectly steady, because the stillness of the wood makes the final squash of our flame easier to see.

Now the line tool gives us those two lovely diagonal logs again. The upper edges are warm dark brown the lower edges charcoal grey and the tiny outer highlights golden brown placed with the pen. I'm deliberately leaving out little cracks and woodgrain, because at this scale the silhouette tells us everything we need to know.

Here comes the soft landing of our bounce. With the solid box tool, I'm making the orange-red lower flame a little wider and shorter, while the bright orange and pale yellow still rise above it. The pen adds a little yellow and orange flicker to the sides, and that wider shape gives our spirit a lovely squash before he stretches upward again.

Finally, the pen gives our little friend two near-black eyes, a dark brown mouth, and two golden yellow sparks near the bottom of the flame. His face has moved down with his body, which helps the whole character feel connected. And when we return to the first frame, that little squash turns naturally into another happy bounce.
Quinn turns the screen to herself to look at her work

Let me turn the screen toward myself and watch our little campfire spirit bounce, friends. I really like how the simple orange and yellow shapes stay recognisable while the flame stretches, settles, and squashes, and how the steady brown logs give the movement a clear reference point. Next time, I might bend the tip of the flame gently from side to side and vary the sparks a little more, giving him an even softer, more playful flicker.
Quinn looks at it and thinks it over
Finished. The animation is playing in FRAMES.

events.html:
Matches my plan: yes
Best part: The flame tip and little face bounce together
Next time: I would add one more tiny squash at the bottom
